chapters.title: Chapter I
paragraphs: JONATHAN HARKER’S JOURNAL
(Written in shorthand.)

3 May. Bistritz.—I left Munich at 8:35 P. M. on 1 May and reached Vienna early the following morning. We were due at 6:46, but the train arrived an hour late. From what I could see through the train window, and during my short walk through its streets, Buda-Pesth looks a wonderful place. I dared not venture far from the station: we had arrived late, and the train would leave as close to its proper time as it could. I had the feeling that we were leaving the West behind and entering the East. The westernmost of the magnificent bridges across the Danube, a river impressively wide and deep here, carried us into a world shaped by the traditions of Turkish rule.

We left reasonably promptly and reached Klausenburgh after dark. I spent the night there at the Hotel Royale. For dinner—or rather supper—I had chicken prepared in some way with red pepper. It tasted very good, but made me thirsty. (Note: get the recipe for Mina.) When I asked the waiter about it, he called it “paprika hendl.” It was a national dish, he said, so I ought to find it anywhere along the Carpathians. The little German I know proved very useful here. In fact, I have no idea how I would manage without it.

While I had some free time in London, I went to the British Museum and searched the library’s books and maps for information about Transylvania. It occurred to me that knowing something about the country beforehand would surely help in my dealings with one of its noblemen. I find that the district he named lies in the far east of the country, where three states meet: Transylvania, Moldavia and Bukovina. It is in the heart of the Carpathian mountains, among the wildest and least-known regions of Europe. I could find no map or book showing the precise location of Castle Dracula. There are no maps of this country yet that can compare with our own Ordnance Survey maps. Bistritz, however, the postal town Count Dracula named, seems to be fairly well known. I shall copy some of my notes here; they may help me remember things when I tell Mina about my travels.

Transylvania’s population consists of four distinct nationalities. In the South are Saxons, and among them the Wallachs, descendants of the Dacians; in the West, Magyars; and in the East and North, Szekelys. It is among this last people that I am going. They say they descend from Attila and the Huns. This may be true: when the Magyars conquered the country in the eleventh century, they found the Huns already settled there. I have read that every superstition known to the world has gathered in the horseshoe formed by the Carpathians, as though this were the centre of a kind of whirlpool of the imagination. If that is so, my stay could be very interesting. (Note: I must ask the Count all about them.)

Despite a comfortable enough bed, I slept badly and had all sorts of strange dreams. A dog howled beneath my window throughout the night, which might explain it. Or perhaps it was the paprika: I drank every drop in my carafe and still felt thirsty. I fell asleep towards morning and woke to persistent knocking at the door, so I suppose by then I must have been sleeping deeply. Breakfast brought more paprika, a kind of maize-flour porridge they called “mamaliga,” and aubergine stuffed with minced meat, a particularly good dish called “impletata.” (Note: get that recipe too.) I had to rush through breakfast because the train left shortly before eight—or was supposed to. After hurrying to the station at 7:30, I sat in the carriage for over an hour before we moved. It seems the farther east one travels, the less punctual the trains become. What can they be like in China?

We seemed to crawl all day through a landscape rich in every kind of beauty. At times we saw little towns or castles perched on steep hilltops, like the pictures in old prayer books. At others we passed rivers and streams whose broad, stony banks on either side suggested heavy flooding. It takes a great quantity of fast-flowing water to scour the outer banks of a river bare. Every station had groups of people, sometimes whole crowds, dressed in all manner of clothes. Some looked just like peasants at home, or those I had seen while travelling through France and Germany: short jackets, round hats, and homemade trousers. Others were remarkably picturesque. The women looked pretty until one came close, but their waists were very bulky. All wore some sort of full white sleeves, and most had broad belts hung with strips of material that fluttered like a ballet costume, though of course they wore petticoats underneath. The strangest people we saw were the Slovaks, more barbarous in appearance than the others. They had large cowboy hats, enormous baggy trousers of a dirty white, white linen shirts, and heavy leather belts almost a foot wide, covered with brass studs. Their trousers were tucked into high boots; their hair was long and black, and their black moustaches thick. They make a striking picture, but hardly an inviting one. On a stage, anyone would immediately take them for an ancient band of Oriental brigands. Yet I am told they are quite harmless, and rather lacking in natural assertiveness.

Twilight was nearly gone when we arrived in Bistritz, a very interesting old town. It stands virtually on the frontier, since the Borgo Pass leads from it into Bukovina. Its history has accordingly been turbulent, and the traces are plain to see. Fifty years ago, a succession of great fires devastated it on five separate occasions. Early in the seventeenth century it endured a three-week siege in which 13,000 people died, famine and disease adding to the losses caused directly by the fighting.

Count Dracula had told me to stay at the Golden Krone Hotel. To my great delight, I found it thoroughly old-fashioned: naturally, I wanted to see as much as possible of the country’s ways. They were plainly expecting me. As I approached the entrance, a cheerful-looking elderly woman appeared in the usual peasant dress: a white undergarment and a long double apron, front and back, of coloured material that fitted almost too tightly for modesty. When I reached her, she bowed. “The Herr Englishman?” “Yes,” I answered, “Jonathan Harker.” With a smile, she said something to an elderly man in white shirt-sleeves who had followed her to the door. He went away and immediately returned carrying a letter:—

“My Friend.—Welcome to the Carpathians. I await your arrival with great eagerness. Sleep well tonight. Tomorrow at three the stagecoach leaves for Bukovina, and a seat has been reserved for you. My carriage will meet you at the Borgo Pass and bring you on to me. I hope your journey from London has been pleasant, and that you will enjoy your visit to my beautiful country.
“Your friend,
“DRACULA.”

4 May.—I discovered that my landlord had received a letter from the Count instructing him to reserve the best seat on the coach for me. But when I asked for details, he grew rather guarded and pretended not to understand my German. That could not be true: until then he had understood me perfectly—or at any rate had answered my questions exactly as though he did. He and his wife, the elderly woman who had welcomed me, exchanged frightened looks. He muttered that the money had come with a letter, and that he knew nothing more. I asked whether he knew Count Dracula and could tell me anything about the castle. Both husband and wife crossed themselves, said they knew absolutely nothing, and refused to speak further. Departure was so close that I had no time to question anyone else. It was all deeply mysterious, and far from reassuring.
Just as I was preparing to leave, the old woman came up to my room and spoke in a state of near hysteria:

“Do you have to go? Oh! young Herr, must you really go?” She was so agitated that she seemed to have forgotten much of her German, mixing it with another language I did not understand at all. Only by asking question after question could I just follow her. I explained that I must leave immediately, because I had important business to attend to. Then she asked me:
“Do you know what day this is?” I told her it was 4 May. Shaking her head, she repeated her question:
“Oh, yes! I know that! I know that—but do you know what day it is?” When I said I did not understand her meaning, she continued:

“It is the eve of St. George’s Day. Don’t you know that tonight, when the clock strikes twelve, every evil thing in the world will have its way? Do you know where you are going, and what you are going to?” She was so obviously distressed that I tried to reassure her, but nothing helped. At last she dropped to her knees and begged me not to go—or at least to postpone my departure for a day or two. It was all quite ridiculous, yet I felt uneasy. Still, I had business to carry out and could let nothing interfere. I tried to help her up and told her as seriously as I could that I was grateful, but my duty allowed no choice: I had to go. She stood up, wiped her eyes, and took a crucifix from her neck to offer me. I did not know how to respond. As a member of the Church of England, I had been taught to regard such things as somewhat idolatrous. Yet refusing an old woman who meant so well, and was so upset, seemed terribly unkind. She must have seen the hesitation on my face. She put the rosary around my neck herself, said, “For your mother’s sake,” and left the room. I am writing this part of my diary as I wait for the coach—which is late, naturally—and the crucifix is still around my neck. I cannot say whether it is the old woman’s terror, the many ghostly traditions here, or the crucifix itself, but my mind is much less at ease than usual. If this book ever reaches Mina before I do, let it carry my farewell. Here is the coach!

5 May. The Castle.—The grey dawn has passed, and the sun stands high above the far horizon. Its outline looks jagged, though whether from trees or hills I cannot tell: at that distance, large things and small blend together. I do not feel sleepy. Since no one is to call me until I wake, I am naturally writing until sleep comes. There are many peculiar things to record. In case anyone reading this imagines that I indulged too freely at dinner before leaving Bistritz, I shall set down exactly what I ate. It was something called “robber steak”: pieces of bacon, onion and beef, seasoned with red pepper, threaded on sticks and roasted over a fire, in the simple style of meat sold for London cats! The wine was Golden Mediasch. It gives a curious, though not unpleasant, sting to the tongue. I had only two glasses, and nothing else to drink.

When I climbed into the coach, the driver had not yet taken his place; I saw him in conversation with the landlady. They were clearly discussing me, for they kept glancing in my direction. Some people sitting on the bench outside the door—a bench whose local name means “word-bearer”—came over to listen, and then looked at me too, most of them with pity. Many words kept recurring, strange words, for the crowd contained people of several nationalities. Quietly, I took my multilingual dictionary from my bag and looked them up. They did nothing to encourage me. Among them were “Ordog”—Satan; “pokol”—hell; “stregoica”—witch; and “vrolok” and “vlkoslak,” which both mean the same thing, one in Slovak and the other in Servian: a creature that is either a werewolf or a vampire. (Note: I must ask the Count about these superstitions.)

As we set off, the crowd outside the inn, now quite large, all crossed themselves and pointed two fingers at me. I had some trouble persuading a fellow passenger to explain these gestures. At first he would not answer, but when he learned I was English, he said they were a charm or protection against the evil eye. This was hardly pleasant, as I was setting out for a place I did not know to meet a man I had never seen. Yet everyone seemed so kind, so sad and so full of sympathy that I could not help being moved. I shall never forget my last view of the inn-yard: those picturesque figures standing around the broad archway, all making the sign of the cross, with the rich leaves of oleanders and orange trees behind them, clustered in green tubs in the middle of the yard. Then our driver cracked his great whip over the four little horses harnessed abreast, and we began our journey. His wide linen trousers—“gotza,” they call them—spread across the whole front of the driver’s seat.

As we drove on, the beauty around us soon made me forget my ghostly fears. Had I understood the language—or rather the languages—of the other passengers, perhaps I could not have shaken them off so readily. Ahead stretched green, sloping country, thick with forests and woods. Here and there, steep hills carried clumps of trees or farmhouses with their windowless gable ends facing the road. Fruit blossom was everywhere in a dazzling profusion: apple, plum, pear and cherry. Passing the trees, I could see fallen petals scattered like stars across the green grass beneath them. The road wound among these green hills, which they call the “Mittel Land,” disappearing around a grassy curve or behind the ragged edges of pine woods that ran down the hillsides like tongues of flame. The surface was rough, yet we seemed to race over it in a fever of haste. I did not then understand the hurry, but the driver plainly meant to reach Borgo Prund without wasting a moment. I was told that the road is excellent in summer, but had not yet been repaired after the winter snow. In that respect it differs from most Carpathian roads: an old tradition says they must not be kept in too good a condition. The Hospadars of former times refused to repair them, for fear the Turk would think they were preparing to admit foreign troops. That might bring forward the war which was, in truth, always ready to break out.

Beyond the green, rounded hills of the Mittel Land, enormous wooded slopes climbed towards the lofty heights of the Carpathians themselves. They towered on both sides of us. The full afternoon sunlight revealed all the magnificent colours of this beautiful range: deep blue and purple in the shadows beneath the peaks, green and brown where grass met rock, and jagged rocks and pointed crags stretching away in an endless succession until they vanished in the distance, where snowy summits rose in splendour. Here and there the mountains seemed split by vast clefts. As the sun began to set, these openings gave us occasional glimpses of the white flash of falling water. We rounded the foot of a hill, and a high, snow-covered mountain peak came into view. One of my companions touched my arm. As our twisting route carried us on, the peak seemed to stand directly ahead:—
“Look! Isten szek!”—“God’s seat!”—he said, reverently making the sign of the cross.

Our winding journey seemed endless. The sun sank lower behind us, and evening shadows began creeping around us. They seemed darker because the snowy mountaintop still caught the sunset and glowed a delicate, cool pink. We passed Cszeks and Slovaks here and there, all in picturesque clothes, though I noticed how distressingly common goitre was among them. Crosses stood all along the roadside, and my companions crossed themselves as we sped past. Occasionally a peasant man or woman knelt before a shrine without even turning at our approach. So complete was their absorption in worship that they seemed blind and deaf to the world outside it. I saw many things unfamiliar to me: haystacks set among the trees, for instance, and beautiful groups of weeping birches, their white trunks shining like silver through the delicate green leaves. Every so often we passed a leiter-wagon, the usual peasant cart, with its long, snakelike backbone designed to follow the uneven road. It invariably carried a group of peasants on their way home. The Cszeks wore white sheepskins, the Slovaks coloured ones; the latter held their long staffs, each ending in an axe, upright like lances. As night approached it grew bitterly cold. In the deepening twilight, the shadows of oak, beech and pine seemed to melt together into one dark haze. But as we climbed through the Pass, dark firs sometimes stood out against lingering snow in the deep valleys between the projecting hills. At times the road cut through pine woods that appeared to close over us in the darkness. Great patches of grey, scattered here and there among the trees, gave the scene a strangely eerie and solemn air. They prolonged the grim imaginings that had begun earlier that evening, when the setting sun threw into startling relief those ghostly clouds which seem always to be winding through the Carpathian valleys. Some hills were so steep that the horses could only climb slowly, however much our driver hurried them. I wanted to get out and walk uphill, as we do at home, but he would not allow it. “No, no,” he said. “You mustn’t walk here; the dogs are too savage.” Then, plainly attempting a grim joke—for he looked around for the others’ approving smiles—he added, “And you may have quite enough of that sort of thing before you get to sleep.” He stopped only long enough to light his lamps.

Once darkness fell, the passengers became visibly excited. One after another they spoke to the driver, apparently pressing him to go faster still. He flogged the horses mercilessly with his long whip, urging them to greater efforts with wild shouts. Ahead, I could make out a patch of grey light in the darkness, as though the hills were divided by a gap. The passengers grew even more agitated. Our rickety coach rocked on its great leather springs, pitching like a boat on a stormy sea, and I had to cling on. The road levelled out, and we seemed to fly. Then the mountains on either side appeared to close in and glare down at us: we were entering the Borgo Pass. Several passengers offered me gifts, one after another, insisting so earnestly that refusal was impossible. The gifts were certainly strange and varied, but each was offered with simple sincerity, a kind word and a blessing. With them came the same curious gestures of fear I had seen outside the Bistritz hotel: the sign of the cross and the protection against the evil eye. As we raced along, the driver bent forward, and passengers on both sides leaned out over the coach’s edge, straining to see into the dark. Clearly something intensely exciting was either happening or expected. I questioned every passenger, but not one would give me any explanation at all. Their excitement lasted for some time. Eventually we saw the eastern side of the Pass opening before us. Dark clouds rolled overhead, and the air felt heavy and oppressive with approaching thunder. It was as though the mountain range divided two different atmospheres and we had now entered the stormy one. By this time I too was watching for the carriage that would take me to the Count. At every moment I expected lamps to shine through the blackness, but everything remained dark. Our own lamps supplied the only light, flickering through the white cloud of steam rising from our hard-driven horses. The sandy road lay pale before us, with no vehicle anywhere in sight. The passengers settled back with a relieved sigh that seemed to mock my disappointment. I had begun considering what to do when the driver glanced at his watch and said something to the others so quietly that I barely caught it. I thought he said, “An hour before the time.” Turning to me, he spoke in German even worse than mine:—

“There is no carriage. The Herr is not expected after all. He will come on to Bukovina now and return tomorrow or the day after. Better the day after.” As he spoke, the horses started neighing, snorting and plunging wildly, forcing him to restrain them. Then, amid screams from the peasants and a general making of the sign of the cross, a four-horse calèche came up from behind, passed us and stopped beside the coach. Our lamps flashed across the horses: magnificent creatures, black as coal. Their driver was a tall man with a long brown beard and a large black hat that seemed to conceal his face. When he turned towards us, all I could make out was a pair of intensely bright eyes, looking red in the lamplight. He addressed our driver:—
“You have arrived early tonight, my friend.” The coachman stammered his answer:—
“The English Herr wanted to hurry.” The stranger answered:—

“That must be why you wanted him to continue to Bukovina, I suppose. You cannot trick me, my friend. I know too much, and my horses are fast.” He smiled as he spoke. In the lamplight I saw a hard mouth, very red lips and teeth that looked sharp and white as ivory. One passenger whispered to another a line from Burger’s “Lenore”:—
“Denn die Todten reiten schnell”— (“For the dead travel fast.”)

The unfamiliar driver evidently caught the words, for he looked up with a brilliant smile. The passenger turned away, extending two fingers and crossing himself at the same time. “Give me the Herr’s luggage,” the driver said. My bags were passed out and placed in the calèche with extraordinary speed. It had stopped close beside us, so I climbed down from the side of the coach. The driver helped me, seizing my arm in a grip like steel; he must have possessed tremendous strength. Without speaking, he shook the reins. The horses turned, and we swept into the darkness of the Pass. Looking back, I saw steam rising from the coach horses in the lamplight, with the figures of my former companions outlined against it as they crossed themselves. Their driver cracked his whip, shouted to his horses, and they raced away towards Bukovina. As they vanished into the dark, a strange chill and a feeling of loneliness came over me. But a cloak was laid over my shoulders and a rug over my knees, and my driver spoke in excellent German:—

“It is a cold night, mein Herr, and my master, the Count, told me to take every care of you. There is a flask of slivovitz—the local plum brandy—under the seat, should you want it.” I drank none, though knowing it was there was comforting all the same. I felt distinctly strange, and considerably frightened. I think I would have chosen any available alternative to continuing that night journey into the unknown. The carriage sped straight ahead; then we turned completely around and travelled along another straight road. I had the impression that we were covering the same ground again and again. I watched for a recognisable landmark and confirmed that we were. I wanted to ask the driver what it meant, but truly I was afraid to. In my position, I thought, any protest would be useless if someone intended to delay me. After a while I grew curious about the time, struck a match and held its light to my watch. It was only a few minutes before midnight. That startled me: I suppose my recent experiences had strengthened the common superstitions about that hour. I waited, sick with suspense.

A dog began howling somewhere at a farmhouse far along the road: a long, agonised wail that sounded full of fear. Another dog answered, then another and another. The wind was now sighing gently through the Pass, carrying a wild chorus of howls that seemed to rise from the whole countryside, as far as my imagination could reach into the dark. At the first cry, the horses strained and reared. The driver spoke soothingly, and they settled, though still trembling and sweating as if they had just bolted in a sudden panic. Then a louder, sharper howling began far away in the mountains on either side: wolves. The horses and I reacted alike. I wanted to leap out of the calèche and run; they reared again and plunged so madly that the driver needed all his immense strength to stop them bolting. Within a few minutes, however, I grew used to the sound, and the horses calmed enough for the driver to climb down and stand before them. He stroked and soothed them, whispering into their ears as horse-tamers are said to do. The effect was extraordinary. Under his touch they became quite manageable, though they still shook. He returned to his seat, shook the reins and drove off at a great speed. This time, after reaching the far side of the Pass, he abruptly turned into a narrow road branching sharply to the right.

Soon trees surrounded us, sometimes arching completely over the road so that we seemed to pass through a tunnel. Elsewhere great, forbidding rocks rose like guards on either side. Though we were sheltered, we heard the strengthening wind moan and whistle among the rocks, while branches crashed together overhead as we raced past. It grew colder and colder. Fine, powdery snow began falling, and soon a white blanket covered both us and everything around us. The cutting wind still brought the dogs’ howls, growing fainter as we travelled. The wolves’ cries, however, drew steadily nearer, as though they were closing in from every direction. I became terribly afraid, and the horses shared my terror. The driver alone remained quite undisturbed. He kept turning his head from side to side, but in the darkness I could see nothing.

Suddenly I noticed a faint blue flame flickering some distance to our left. The driver saw it at the same instant. He immediately reined in the horses, jumped down and disappeared into the dark. I had no idea what to do, especially as the wolves’ cries were coming closer. While I was wondering, he abruptly reappeared, took his seat without speaking, and drove on. I think I must have fallen asleep and repeatedly dreamed the same incident, for it seemed to happen over and over without end. Looking back now, it has the quality of a dreadful nightmare. Once the flame appeared so close to the road that even in the surrounding darkness I could follow the driver’s movements. He hurried to the spot where the blue light rose. It must have been extremely faint, since it did not seem to light the ground around it at all. He gathered a few stones and arranged them in a pattern. At one point there was a strange trick of vision: when he stood between me and the flame, he did not block it. I could still see its ghostly flicker through him. This startled me, but it lasted only a moment, so I assumed my eyes had deceived me as I strained to see in the dark. For a while after that, no blue flames appeared. We sped through the blackness, surrounded by the wolves’ howling as though they were following us in a travelling circle.

At last the driver went farther from the carriage than he had gone before. While he was away, the horses began shaking more violently than ever, snorting and screaming in fear. I could see no reason for it: the wolves had stopped howling altogether. Just then the moon sailed out through the black clouds, appearing behind the jagged crest of an overhanging rock covered in pines. Its light revealed a ring of wolves surrounding us. They had white teeth, dangling red tongues, long sinewy limbs and shaggy coats. In that grim silence they were a hundred times more terrifying than they had been when howling. I felt almost paralysed with fear. Only when a man finds himself face to face with such horrors can he understand what they really mean.

Without warning the wolves began howling again, as if the moonlight had affected them in some strange way. The horses plunged and reared, looking helplessly around with eyes that rolled so desperately it hurt to watch. But the living ring of terror enclosed them on every side, and there was no escape. I called for the driver. Our only chance, it seemed to me, was to try to break through that ring and help him reach us. I shouted and hammered the side of the calèche, hoping the noise would drive back the wolves on that side and leave him a way to the carriage. I have no idea how he got there, but suddenly I heard his voice lifted in a tone of absolute command. Turning towards it, I saw him standing in the road. He swept his long arms through the air as though clearing away some invisible obstruction, and the wolves retreated, farther and farther. At that moment a heavy cloud covered the moon, plunging us into darkness again.

When I could see once more, the driver was climbing into the calèche and the wolves were gone. Everything was so strange and unnatural that a terrible fear seized me; I dared neither speak nor move. Time seemed without end as we drove on, now in almost total darkness, with rolling clouds hiding the moon. We continued climbing, broken occasionally by a swift descent, but always going higher overall. Suddenly I realised that the driver was bringing the horses to a halt in the courtyard of an enormous ruined castle. Not a single ray of light showed in its tall black windows, and its broken battlements cut a jagged outline against the moonlit sky.
